analysis.one_liner: Lets private employers give hourly workers paid time off instead of cash overtime pay.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 225-195 on July 30, 1996, but the Senate never voted and it died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have changed federal overtime law so a private employer could offer an hourly worker 1.5 hours of paid time off for every overtime hour worked, instead of the cash overtime pay the law now requires, if the worker agreed in writing. Unused time off would be capped at 240 hours and paid out in cash at year's end or when the worker left the job. The House passed it on a near-party-line vote, but the Senate never brought it up before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Hourly workers who would rather have time off than extra cash, such as parents juggling childcare, would gain a new option, though only if they agreed to it in writing. Employers would gain scheduling flexibility and the ability to cover overtime hours with time off instead of cash.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hourly workers wanting time off, and their employers

how_it_helps.text: An employee could choose compensatory time off at a rate of at least one and a half hours for each overtime hour, in place of overtime pay.

Accrued compensatory time was capped at 240 hours, and any time not used by the end of the year or at termination of employment had to be paid out in cash at the higher of the worker's average or final regular pay rate.
Employers were barred from intimidating, threatening, or coercing workers to choose or use compensatory time, with violations carrying an equal amount in liquidated damages.
A private-sector worker could withdraw the agreement at any time and, by written request, demand cash payment within 30 days for all compensatory time accrued but not yet used.

Employers could only provide compensatory time through an agreement with employee representatives, or with an individual employee who signed a verifiable written statement, and the agreement could not be a condition of employment.

analysis.who_pays: Employers would bear the cost of granting time off at 1.5 times overtime hours and paying out unused time in cash at year's end or on termination. Workers who chose time off would forgo the extra cash income overtime now provides, and could end up with a bank of time off their employer might not let them use when they want it.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers, and workers who trade cash for time

drawbacks.text: An employer could refuse a worker's request to actually use the accrued time off if doing so would "unduly disrupt" operations, so the promised time away from work was not guaranteed.

In non-union workplaces, the required agreement is made directly with the employer, and critics, including organized labor, warned this structure would let employers pressure workers into accepting time off instead of the cash their families may need.
An employer could discontinue its compensatory time policy, or cash out a worker's accrued time above 80 hours, on 30 days' notice, so the arrangement could be ended or converted unilaterally.
A worker living paycheck to paycheck who took compensatory time in place of overtime would see less take-home pay in those weeks, with the cash value deferred to year's end.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For some workers, the chance to bank 1.5 hours of time off per overtime hour is genuinely valuable, and the bill included real guardrails: a written opt-in, a 240-hour cap, cash payout at year's end or on leaving, an anti-coercion rule backed by double damages, and the right to withdraw at any time. The serious weakness is enforcement in practice: because the employer controls when time off can be used and can exit the arrangement on short notice, a worker in a non-union shop may face pressure to accept time off they cannot actually take, trading guaranteed cash overtime for a promise. How much ordinary workers gained or lost would have depended heavily on how vigorously the anti-coercion and payout rules were enforced.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the House 225-195, but the Senate never brought it to a vote before the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in September 1995 and referred to the House Committee on Economic and Educational Opportunities, which ordered it reported on a 20-16 vote and reported it amended on July 11, 1996.
A House rule (H. Res. 488) set the terms of debate, and the House passed the bill on July 30, 1996, by a vote of 225 to 195.
The vote split almost entirely by party: 211 of 235 Republicans voted yes while only 14 of 198 Democrats did.
The Senate received the bill on July 31, 1996, read it twice, and placed it on its calendar, but it never came to a vote before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a Senate vote, employers did not gain the option of covering overtime with time off instead of cash, and hourly workers kept the existing guarantee of cash overtime pay. Organized labor, which had campaigned against the bill, preserved the overtime standard it defends.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hourly workers kept guaranteed cash overtime

for.name: Cass Ballenger
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, spoke for it on the floor, and shepherded it through subcommittee and full committee.

for.name: William Goodling
for.role: Chair, House Committee on Economic and Educational Opportunities
for.what_they_did: His committee marked up and reported the bill on a 20-16 vote, and he handled the bill's substitute amendment during floor debate.

for.name: House Republican leaders
for.role: House Rules Committee and floor managers
for.what_they_did: Brought the rule (H. Res. 488) to the floor and scheduled the bill for a July 30, 1996 vote under a structured debate.

for.name: President Bill Clinton
for.what_they_did: Opposed the bill, and its opponents cited the threat of a veto as the reason the Senate never took it up.

for.name: Labor unions (AFL-CIO)
for.what_they_did: Campaigned against the bill, calling it a threat to cash overtime pay for hourly workers.

against.name: Senate leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a Senate floor vote after it was placed on the Senate calendar.

sides.party_line_note: The July 30, 1996 House vote split almost entirely by party: 211 of 235 Republicans voted yes, while only 14 of 198 Democrats joined them; 19 Republicans and the chamber's one Independent voted no.

industries.industry: Private employers of hourly workers (retail, food service, manufacturing)
industries.note: The bill would have let these employers cover overtime hours with paid time off instead of cash, gaining scheduling flexibility and deferring cash payouts. Workers kept the right to opt out and demand cash, so the employer's gain did not automatically come at workers' expense, but critics warned the arrangement could be used to pressure workers out of overtime income.

In unionized workplaces, compensatory time could only be provided through a collective bargaining agreement, so unions retained control over whether it was offered at all. Union leaders nonetheless opposed the bill as a threat to the cash-overtime standard they enforce, and its death preserved that standard.

The bill largely carried forward the existing system under which government employers can already offer compensatory time, with higher accrual caps (480 hours) for public safety, emergency, and seasonal workers, so the public-sector status quo was written into the new framework.
